Lieutenant James Allen of the U.S. Army is appointed Superintendent of the harbour works at Chicago. The column is interleaved with the prairie-description column beside it line for line, so `lines_of_claim` names only the lines this paragraph can be followed through; the rest of the range is the neighbour's. What it fixes for a reconstruction is a date and an agency: from February 1834 the works have an officer of their own rather than the commanding officer at Fort Dearborn doing it alongside the garrison, and the pier that is crossing the bar by August 1834 (1834-08-13, claim c001) is built under him.

claims.notes: THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IS IN USE AS A PUBLIC HALL five weeks after its dedication, which the January read recorded (1834-01-21, claim c002 there). That is the fact this claim carries for the model: the building this project already has stands, and the town's societies meet in it on a weekday evening. It also names eleven men at once — the officers of the Chicago Temperance Society for 1834 — with two physicians as president and vice-president, the druggist Philo Carpenter as secretary, and three serving officers of the garrison on the executive committee, which is a measure of how far Fort Dearborn's people were part of the town's civil life eighteen months before the scene date. The next meeting is set for Tuesday 25 February, which is the day of the last issue in this month's range.

claims.notes: A BUILDING WITH A PLACEMENT AND A PAST USE, and both are worth having. It stood OPPOSITE THE BRIDGE OVER THE NORTH BRANCH — one of the two plank-and-timber bridges the November 1833 ordinances legislated about — and it had been the town's MEETING HOUSE before the Presbyterian church was dedicated in January 1834. So this is where the congregation met until five weeks ago, and it is being auctioned as a lot improvement in the same sale as two platted lots. The lots are named to block and half-lot (west half of Lot 3, Block 44; Lot 7, Block 8), which almost nothing else in this corpus does. NOT PLACED IN THE MODEL by this claim: 'opposite the bridge' names a side of the river and not a lot, and the North Branch bridge's own position is a separate question this project has open.

claims.notes: THE BRIDGES, SPECIFIED IN TIMBER SIZES — the most useful single reading in this issue for anything that has to be built. The January read has the trustees ordering a contract for the bridges on 4 December 1833 and the December read corrected 'building' to REPAIRING; this is the advertisement that contract produced, and it says what the repair consisted of: braces of oak 6 inches square for each bridge, a NEW BENT to the south bridge, oak railing 8 by 4 inches, oak standards 4 feet high, flooring of oak plank 2 inches thick, secured to the plank by oak pins 1 1/2 inches in diameter and 2 feet long, railing spiked or pinned. Every dimension is the paper's own. THE COLUMN EDGE HAS EATEN THE COUNTS — how many braces, how far apart the standards — and those are left as gaps rather than guessed, because a number is exactly the kind of thing a reconstruction would then build to. The money is payable wholly on 15 August 1834, which dates the work to the season between.

That is about a mile and a half north-west of the platted town, on the North Branch, and it is the only industrial building of its size this corpus places at all. It matters for the fabric question the whole project turns on: a steam sawmill within two miles means SAWN boards were available in Chicago in 1834 and not only hewn timber and imported lumber, which is what the price current's 'Lumber, poplar ass'd' at 20 to 23 dollars the thousand feet is priced against. The notice is dated 'January 8, 1833' in the transcription; the year is read as 1833 as printed and NOT corrected, because a standing advertisement carrying last year's dateline is ordinary and a silent correction would invent a date.

claims.notes:
A TAVERN CHANGES HANDS, THE NEW KEEPER DOES NOT SIGN, AND THE OUTGOING MAN'S GIVEN NAME IS NOT SETTLED. The advertisement calls the house a NOTED tavern stand, names the man going out as W. Wattles, and never says where it is or who the subscriber is; it is printed unchanged in all four February issues and in the December ones before them. Recorded because the succession is a fact and the silence is a finding: this is the shape of the corpus's hardest business claims, a real house in the town with no address and no proprietor, and it is entered with placement `none` rather than guessed at.

THE GIVEN NAME, AND WHY IT IS LEFT OPEN. The January read (1834-01-28, claim c009) normalizes the same standing advertisement to '[Jo]hn W. Wattles', with the first two letters SUPPLIED — that printing had lost them too. All three February printings that carry the line legibly set an initial H: 'Mr, Hin. Watihs' here, 'Mr, Hs W, Wattles' on the 11th, 'Mr. Him. W. Wattles' on the 18th. So the February evidence is for HIRAM and the January evidence is a supply, and neither is a reading of surviving type. It is entered here as '[uncertain: H…] W. Wattles' rather than resolved either way, because this corpus's identity policy refuses to merge one surname across two initials without a stated rule and NO RULE IS AVAILABLE: the question is what the page said, and only the page images can answer it. Both entries stand in the gazetteer until they do.

claims.notes:
THE FIRST HALF OF THE 1 JANUARY 1834 CHICAGO LETTER LIST, A TO H, AND THIS IS THE PRINTING IT IS MINTED FROM. Ruling 1 applies in full: this is Chicago's own post office, so every listed name mints a resident candidate flagged `letter_list_only`.

WHY MINT FROM A FOURTH PRINTING OF A LIST ALREADY READ. The January read (T-0310) minted 97 names from 1834-01-28 and said in terms that 97 was a FLOOR, not the printed length: the .docx extraction there crushed the printed list's two alphabetical columns into eight paragraph lines and left orphan debris where names stood. That gap is the open ticket T-0318, whose stated route to closing it was the page images. IT DOES NOT NEED THEM. The list is printed AGAIN in all four February issues, from ruled .txt transcriptions that carry ONE NAME PER LINE, and this column is the best surviving witness for its first half — 74 lines of it, initials intact. Seventy-two names are minted here, of which the great majority were unreadable or absent in the January witness.

THE MINTING RULE, so the same list is not minted six times (the defect T-0299 records): ONE LIST, ONE COHORT. The list is minted ONCE per half, each half from the single printing that carries it best — this column for A-H, and 1834-02-11 page 4 column 3 for H-W. The other four February printings of the same list are recorded as REPRINTS with their names UNMINTED, exactly as the October 1834 read handled its three printings. Names that also stand in the January minting merge on the normalized name and add a mention rather than a person.

WHAT IS STILL LOST. The printed list ran in TWO alphabetical sub-columns and the segmenter kept only the left one whole; the right one survives as line-end debris ('Edwar', 'Isanc K', 'Lewis |') and is quoted with the rest but read as nothing. So this is a floor too, and it is a much higher one. The row for 'Et halet Atkins' and two others are left in uncertainty brackets because no February printing agrees on them.

claims.notes: A TAVERN EIGHTEEN MILES OUT ON THE OTTAWA ROAD, and it is recorded precisely because it is NOT in the town. The reconstruction stands inside the plat; this is a stage house on the road the 18 February coach advertisement times at three and a half days from Ottawa. Its value here is that it establishes what the road south-west was carrying in the winter of 1833-34 — travellers wanting corn and oats for their horses — and it is a reminder to the next pass that 'Chicago' in this paper's advertising columns often means the county.
